title: Nitrites in Urine: What a Positive or Negative Result Means
summary: Nitrites in urine usually mean bacteria, but not always a UTI. Learn how to read nitrite with leukocytes, WBC and epithelial cells, and what happens next.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


**Nitrites in urine usually mean bacteria are present in the urinary tract, and with urinary symptoms a positive nitrite strongly suggests a urinary tract infection (UTI).** Nitrite forms when bacteria convert nitrate, a chemical normally present in urine, into nitrite, so it is not normally found in urine \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/nitrites-in-urine/) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003579.htm) \]\[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]. A positive result is a fairly reliable sign of bacteria. A negative result does not rule out an infection \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/nitrites-in-urine/) \]\[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \].


The nitrite line also does not stand alone. It is read next to leukocyte esterase, the microscopic white blood cell count, bacteria and epithelial cells on the same urinalysis, and next to whether you have symptoms \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/nitrites-in-urine/) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. When bacteria are in the urine without symptoms, guidelines advise against treating them in most people, with pregnancy and certain urologic procedures as the main exceptions \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000520.htm) \]. A urine culture confirms which bacteria are growing \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003751.htm) \].


## What the urine nitrite test detects


The nitrite test is a pad on a urine dipstick, read as positive or negative as part of a routine urinalysis \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/nitrites-in-urine/) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. It does not detect bacteria directly. It detects nitrite, which many bacteria produce from urinary nitrate \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/nitrites-in-urine/) \]\[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \].


Many gram-negative bacteria and some gram-positive bacteria can make this conversion \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]. A positive dipstick nitrite indicates these organisms are present in significant numbers, more than 10,000 per mL \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]. On a Mito report this result appears as[urine nitrite](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-nitrite) .


Two features of how nitrite forms explain most confusing results:


- **It takes time.** Bacteria need about four hours in the bladder to produce nitrites \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. Urine that has not sat in the bladder long enough can read negative even when bacteria are present \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].
- **Not every bacterium makes it.** Some bacteria, such as Enterococcus, do not produce nitrite \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].


## What a positive nitrite result means


**A positive nitrite in someone with urinary symptoms strongly suggests a UTI** \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. Nitrite is more specific for a UTI than leukocyte esterase \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. In a summary of studies, mostly of adult women seen in emergency departments, a positive nitrite had a positive likelihood ratio of 13 for a UTI, the highest of any single urinalysis finding \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. An earlier review reported a nitrite specificity of 92 to 100% against culture-confirmed UTI \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \].


Common UTI symptoms include pain or burning when urinating, a strong need to urinate often, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, and pressure or cramping in the lower abdomen \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \].


A positive nitrite is still a screening result. A meta-analysis of dipstick studies concluded that positive dipstick results need to be confirmed, and that the dipstick alone is doubtful for ruling an infection in \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15175113/) \]. The usual confirmation is a urine culture, which grows bacteria from the sample and identifies them, usually within 24 to 48 hours \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003751.htm) \].


## Reading nitrite with the rest of the urinalysis


A urinalysis has several lines that relate to infection. Each answers a different question, and together they tell you more than nitrite alone.


Report line What it shows How it changes the nitrite reading


Nitrite (dipstick) Nitrite made by bacteria \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/nitrites-in-urine/) \]\[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \] Specific but misses many infections \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[Leukocyte esterase](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-leukocytes) (dipstick) An enzyme from white blood cells, a sign of inflammation or infection \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \] Positive with positive nitrite suggests a UTI. Negative together with a negative nitrite makes a UTI less likely \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]\[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15175113/) \]


[White blood cells](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-white-blood-cells) (microscopy, WBC/HPF) White cells counted under a microscope per high-power field \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \] More than 5 WBC/HPF is consistent with a UTI in someone with symptoms \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[Bacteria](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-bacteria) (microscopy) Bacteria seen in the sample \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \] Seen with both infection and contamination, so a culture is needed to identify a dominant species \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[Squamous epithelial cells](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-epithelial-cells-non-renal) (microscopy) Skin-type cells from the outer urethra and the vulva \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \] More than 5 per high-power field suggests the sample was contaminated, which can make the nitrite and bacteria lines less reliable \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


Some combinations you may see:


- **Positive nitrite, positive leukocyte esterase, white cells present, with symptoms.** This is the classic UTI pattern \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. A culture identifies the bacteria \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/nitrites-in-urine/) \]\[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003751.htm) \].
- **Positive nitrite, many squamous epithelial cells.** The sample may be contaminated with bacteria from the skin \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. A repeat clean-catch sample helps. Even with contamination, white cells or blood in the urine still suggest a UTI \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].
- **Positive nitrite, no leukocyte esterase, no white cells, no symptoms.** This can be bacteria in the urine without infection (see below), contamination or a false positive \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000520.htm) \].
- **Negative nitrite, negative leukocyte esterase.** When both are negative, a UTI is much less likely. In the review above, this combination had a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. The meta-analysis found that both tests being negative was useful to exclude infection in most groups \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15175113/) \].


## Negative nitrite with leukocytes in urine


**A negative nitrite with positive leukocyte esterase can still be a UTI.** Nitrite is specific but not very sensitive, so a negative result does not rule out infection \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]. The earlier review reported nitrite sensitivity of only 19 to 48% for culture-confirmed UTI \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]. Three reasons explain most of the misses:


- **Bacteria that do not make nitrite.** Enterococcus is one example \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].
- **Short time in the bladder.** Bacteria need about four hours in the bladder to make nitrite, so frequent urination often gives a false negative \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].
- **Dilute urine or interference.** High urine specific gravity and vitamin C can cause a false-negative nitrite \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. In a study of culture-confirmed Enterobacterales infections that tested nitrite negative, the authors named dilute urine and vitamin C among the likely causes, and concluded that a standard urine culture is needed to rule out a UTI \[[10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36762527/) \].


Leukocytes without nitrites can also have a cause other than a bladder infection. Leukocyte esterase is present with inflammation and infection more generally, including sexually transmitted infections \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. White cells in the urine can come from kidney stones \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. Other causes of white cells with a negative culture include urethritis, viral infections, bladder tumors, exercise and glomerulonephritis \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]. Contamination of the sample can also turn the leukocyte esterase pad positive \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].


So with leukocytes but no nitrites, symptoms matter most. With urinary symptoms, a urine culture is the next step \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. Without symptoms, a repeat clean-catch sample is a reasonable way to check whether the finding persists.


## Nitrites in urine but no UTI


**Bacteria in the urine do not always mean an infection.** Asymptomatic bacteriuria means bacteria are growing in the urine but there are no urinary symptoms \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000520.htm) \]. The Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) defines it in a voided sample as 100,000 or more colony-forming units per mL on culture, whether or not white cells are also present \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \].


It is a common finding in many groups, including healthy women \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \]. A positive nitrite, which reflects bacteria, can therefore appear in someone with no infection to treat.


The 2019 IDSA guideline recommends against screening for or treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \]:


- healthy premenopausal, nonpregnant women and healthy postmenopausal women;
- people with diabetes;
- older adults living in the community who are functionally impaired, and older adults in long-term care.


The guideline recommends screening and treatment in two main situations: pregnancy, and before endoscopic urologic procedures that injure the lining of the urinary tract \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \]. MedlinePlus lists a few other situations, such as a recent kidney transplant \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000520.htm) \]. The reason for restraint is that treating bacteria that cause no harm adds to unnecessary antibiotic use, which promotes antibiotic resistance \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \], and can make later infections harder to treat \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000520.htm) \].


Bacteria in the urine is not the only explanation for a positive nitrite without symptoms. The pad can also turn positive from a contaminated sample, a dipstick exposed to air, or phenazopyridine \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. Strips left exposed to air give false positives often: after one week of exposure, about one third of strips read positive, and after two weeks about three quarters \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \].


Whether a positive nitrite without symptoms needs follow-up depends on your situation, which is a question for your doctor. Pregnancy and a planned urologic procedure are the clearest reasons to follow it up even without symptoms \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000520.htm) \].


## Nitrites in urine during pregnancy


**Pregnancy is the main exception to leaving symptom-free bacteria alone.** The IDSA guideline strongly recommends screening for and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnant women \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \]. To diagnose it, a urine sample is sent for culture \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000520.htm) \].


In a meta-analysis of dipstick accuracy, the nitrite test was highly accurate in studies of pregnant women \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15175113/) \]. It is still a screen, and the culture is what confirms bacteriuria and guides any treatment \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000520.htm) \]\[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003751.htm) \]. A positive nitrite in pregnancy should go to your prenatal clinician, who decides on culture and treatment. Pregnant people with a UTI and a fever, or who feel ill, may need hospital care \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \].


## False positives and false negatives


Dipstick results can be wrong in both directions \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]:


Result Common causes


False-positive nitrite Contaminated sample, a dipstick exposed to air, phenazopyridine \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


False-negative nitrite Bacteria that do not reduce nitrate, short time in the bladder, high urine specific gravity, vitamin C \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


Handling matters too. Delays of more than two hours between collection and examination often make urinalysis results unreliable, so urine that cannot be examined promptly should be refrigerated \[[3](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \].


## What happens next after a nitrite result


1. **Match the result to your symptoms.** A positive nitrite with urinary symptoms points to a UTI \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. Without symptoms, bacteria may be present without infection \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000520.htm) \].
2. **Read the other infection lines.** Look at leukocyte esterase, the microscopic white cell count, bacteria and squamous epithelial cells, as in the table above \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].
3. **Repeat a clean sample when the result is unclear.** For UTI testing, a midstream clean-catch sample is the standard \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. If many squamous cells suggest contamination, a repeat clean-catch sample gives a more reliable reading \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].
4. **Get a urine culture when an infection is suspected.** A culture is recommended when UTI symptoms are present \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. It identifies the bacteria and helps decide which treatment, if any, is needed \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/nitrites-in-urine/) \]\[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003751.htm) \]. Results take 24 to 48 hours \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003751.htm) \].

## When to get prompt care


**Contact your doctor if you have symptoms of a UTI** \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]. **Contact them right away** if you have signs that an infection may have reached the kidneys \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]:


- back or side pain;
- fever or chills;
- vomiting.


Also get in touch if UTI symptoms come back shortly after treatment \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]. In older people, confusion or other mental changes can be the only sign of a UTI \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]. If you are pregnant, contact your prenatal clinician about any positive nitrite or urinary symptoms, and seek care promptly for fever or feeling ill \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \]\[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \].

## Frequently asked questions


### What causes positive nitrites in urine?


Nitrites form when bacteria in the urine convert nitrate, a chemical normally found in urine, into nitrite. Many of the bacteria that cause urinary tract infections can do this, so a positive nitrite usually means bacteria are present in significant numbers. A positive result can also come from a contaminated sample, a test strip that was left exposed to air, or the medicine phenazopyridine. A urine culture confirms whether bacteria are really growing and which ones.


### Can you have nitrites in urine but no UTI?


Yes. Some people have bacteria in their urine without any urinary symptoms, which is called asymptomatic bacteriuria. It is a common finding, including in healthy women. The Infectious Diseases Society of America advises against screening for or treating it in most people, with pregnancy and certain urologic procedures as the main exceptions. A positive nitrite can also come from a contaminated sample or a strip exposed to air.


### What kills nitrites in urine?


Nitrite is not a germ. It is a chemical that bacteria make in the bladder, so it disappears from urine when the bacteria making it are gone. A later negative nitrite is not proof that an infection has cleared, though: frequent urination, dilute urine, vitamin C and bacteria that do not make nitrite can all give a negative result while bacteria are still present. When it matters, a urine culture after treatment is the test that checks whether the bacteria are gone.


### What does leukocytes but no nitrites in urine mean?


Leukocyte esterase is a sign of white blood cells. With a negative nitrite it can still be a urinary tract infection, because some bacteria, such as Enterococcus, do not make nitrite and because nitrite needs about four hours in the bladder to form. It can also come from a contaminated sample, a sexually transmitted infection, kidney stones or other inflammation. Symptoms, the microscopic white cell count and a urine culture decide which.


### Are nitrites in urine during pregnancy serious?


Nitrites in pregnancy should always be followed up with your prenatal clinician, even without symptoms. Pregnancy is one of the few situations where guidelines recommend screening for and treating bacteria in the urine when there are no symptoms, because the risks of an untreated infection are higher. A urine culture confirms the result before any decision about treatment.
